records.issue_text: [Low/bug] Regression in office365calendar: the previous code logged the zod error plus the provider response and continued after a failed token parse; parseRefreshTokenResponse now throws a generic "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned", removing diagnostic context and turning previously non-fatal parse failures into hard failures.
records.rationale: The diff shows office365calendar previously logged the zod error and MS response on parse failure and continued (`tokenResponse.error`, `MS response` logging removed, and `tokenResponse.safeParse` replaced by `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, whose failure path throws `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")`). This confirms the described mechanism: non-fatal parse failures become hard throws and diagnostics are lost. Whether this regression is harmful vs. an intentional tightening is debatable, but the behavior change is real and verifiable in the diff.

records.issue_text: [Low/data] The decrypted keys are persisted as credential.key without being validated against the app's credential schema, so a wrong-keyed or malformed payload silently poisons the credential and only fails later at runtime.
records.rationale: Verifiable in the diff: in app-credential.ts, the decrypted payload is `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...))` and written directly via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: keys } })` / `create` with no schema validation, unlike the normal OAuth paths which zod-parse credentials (e.g. googleCredentialSchema.parse). This is a specific, grounded gap, but the input comes from a trusted, secret-authenticated parent application, so it is a data-integrity/validation hardening concern rather than clearly broken behavior introduced by the change.

records.issue_text: [Medium/bug] The lenient schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse is selected purely from env vars rather than whether the sync path was actually taken: with sync enabled, responses obtained directly from providers are also minimally parsed and stripped — e.g. salesforce CalendarService persists a stripped Salesforce token (losing instance_url, signature, etc. that jsforce needs), and team credentials (userId null → local refresh) are corrupted the same way.
records.rationale: parseRefreshTokenResponse selects minimumTokenResponseSchema based solely on APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED env, not on whether refreshOAuthTokens actually took the sync path (which also requires CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT and non-null userId). The diff shows Salesforce CalendarService calling parseRefreshTokenResponse unconditionally, and when sharing is enabled it would strip Salesforce token fields (instance_url, signature, etc.) and persist the stripped key via prisma.credential.update — a real data-loss defect visible in the diff.

records.issue_text: [Medium/concurrency] The findFirst-then-create/update sequence in app-credential.ts has a TOCTOU race: two concurrent webhook calls for the same (userId, appId) can both find nothing and both create, producing duplicate credentials; there is no unique constraint or upsert.
records.rationale: The diff's app-credential.ts handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst` on (userId, appId) and then conditionally `create` or `update`, with no transaction, no upsert (the code even comments 'Can't use prisma upsert'), and no unique constraint shown anywhere in the diff. Two concurrent webhook calls for the same user/app can both pass findFirst and both create duplicate credentials. This is a verifiable correctness defect introduced by the new endpoint.

records.issue_text: [Medium/performance] A Salesforce token refresh (network call) plus a credential DB write now run unconditionally on every service instantiation (i.e. every calendar/booking operation) instead of only when the token is expired as jsforce's lazy refresh previously did — extra Salesforce API traffic, DB write churn, and transient refresh failures now break every operation.
records.rationale: The diff adds an unconditional `fetch("https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token" ...)` plus a `prisma.credential.update` in the SalesforceCalendarService constructor path (before `return new jsforce.Connection(...)`), with no expiry check shown — so a token refresh and DB write now execute on every service instantiation, whereas jsforce previously handled refresh lazily via its own connection options. This is a verifiable performance/behavioral regression introduced by the diff.
